Short impact summary

Focal motility determines the geometry of dendritic spines☆ (2003) in Neuroscience. 39 citations.

Full narrative

Focal motility determines the geometry of dendritic spines☆ (2003) in Neuroscience is authored by Martijn Roelandse, Arkadiusz Welman and Uta Wagner. Topics: Dendritic filopodia, Dendritic spine, Filopodia, Lamellipodium and Excitatory postsynaptic potential.

39 citations (OpenAlex). Citations peaked in 2005 with 5 citing works. Citing venues include Journal of Neuroscience, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences and European Journal of Neuroscience.

Limited online visibility beyond citations.
narrative_llm:
Short impact summary

This 2003 Neuroscience article has seen clear scholarly uptake, with 39 OpenAlex citations and 40 documented downstream reuses. Its influence is concentrated in neuroscience and synaptic biology, and the citing record shows that the paper has remained relevant to later work on dendritic spines, filopodia, and structural plasticity. The strongest trace of community reception is academic rather than public, with one supporting scite citation statement and only a minimal public-discourse signal.

Full narrative

Roelandse, Welman, Wagner, Hagmann, and Matus published this article at a time when the mechanisms shaping dendritic spine geometry were an active problem in cell and synaptic neuroscience. The paper’s concept profile centers on dendritic filopodia, dendritic spines, filopodia, and actin remodeling, matching its focus on how focal motility contributes to spine form. That topical framing appears to have given the work a durable role as a mechanistic reference point for later studies of neuronal structure and plasticity.

The citation record shows steady academic use. OpenAlex lists 39 citations, and the article’s citing venues include established neuroscience outlets such as the Journal of Neuroscience, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, European Journal of Neuroscience, Neuroscience, and Frontiers in Synaptic Neuroscience. The citing literature is largely article-based, with some dissertations and book chapters, suggesting that the paper has been used both as a research reference and as background in longer-form scholarly synthesis.

The downstream reuse graph reinforces that pattern: 40 reuse events are documented, overwhelmingly in articles, with additional appearances in dissertations, book chapters, and one review. Later citing works span topics from dendritic spine ultrastructure and filopodia-driven plasticity to broader discussions of synaptic architecture and neural interfaces, indicating that the article’s contribution has been absorbed into adjacent methodological and conceptual conversations rather than remaining confined to a narrow subfield.

Public attention appears limited in the available record, with no broader event-data discussion captured and only one newsfeed mention. That modest public footprint does not diminish the paper’s scholarly role; rather, it suggests that its impact has been primarily technical and disciplinary, carried through citation, reuse, and incorporation into the neuroscience literature. Overall, the record supports a picture of a focused but enduring contribution to the study of dendritic spine morphogenesis.
